clue.text: £51 uncle's blown, consuming hot 'meals' that are really just booze

a quid is British slang for one pound

explanation.surface: An uncle has blown fifty-one pounds on so-called meals that are really just drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: The £ sign has to be read as a word, QUID (a pound in British slang), and 51 as the Roman numeral LI; these join UNCLES as the anagram fodder, with H slipped in.
explanation.definitionFit: A liquid lunch is a jokey idiom for a midday break spent drinking alcohol instead of eating food.

clue.text: Behold! 'New joke' at first originated in ancient past

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'New joke' make it look like one phrase, but it splits into N and GAG.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are adverbial expressions placing an event far back in time, many years before now.

clue.text: Low-carb diet's sound in Ecuador's capital

explanation.definitionFit: The city is the seat of government of Ecuador, high in the Andes, and so its national capital.

taken as written

clue.text: Opposed to Protestantism to some extent

explanation.definitionFit: Edward Heath, known as Ted, led the UK government as Conservative prime minister in the early 1970s.

clue.text: Message in very odd parts of zodiac wanting flipping Everyman to irritate

clue.text: Citron mixed with water in French drink

clue.text: Cheerful boy, by George (to begin with)

clue.text: Primarily, someone honouring 'Infallible Ali'?
